title: Tactics
subtitle: The four motifs that decide games

blocks.title: Tactics do not fall from the sky
blocks.text: Capablanca was above all a positional player, and yet he finished his games with combinations — because a combination is not invented. It appears only once the position has ripened for it: when two enemy pieces line up on the same line, diagonal or knight's leap, or when they are left undefended. Tactics serve the plan, not the other way round.

A tactical motif is a **shape** that keeps coming back. You do not learn it by heart, you recognise it — the way you recognise a face. Here are the four basic ones: the **fork**, the **pin**, the **skewer** and the **discovered attack**. Three of them make **two threats at once**, and your opponent can only answer one of them with a single move; the pin makes a single threat but takes away the defender that would meet it. What they share is that no one move answers everything. In all four exercises below it is White to move.

A **fork** is one piece attacking two targets at the same moment. Your opponent saves one and loses the other. The knight is the most dangerous piece for this: it jumps over everything, so there is no blocking its attack — the target has to run. The purest form is the fork **with check**: the king must step aside, and the second target is left with no help.

blocks.title: Knight fork
blocks.hint: The knight is looking for a square that hits two targets at once.
blocks.solvedMessage: Nd4+ and then Nxc2 — the rook falls. ✓
blocks.wrongMessage: Not that one — look for a double attack.
blocks.playingPrompt: Play the move that makes a fork.

blocks.text: A **pin** is when a piece may not move because something more valuable stands behind it on the same line. If what stands behind it is the **king**, moving **off that line** is not merely bad but illegal. That is why a pinned piece is a defender in appearance only: the square it "guards" is not really guarded. The same goes for interposing: to step in the way, a pinned piece would have to leave its line — and that it may not do. Before you break through or sacrifice, check whether the defender is pinned.

blocks.title: The pinned defender
blocks.hint: One black defender is pinned — strike where it is not allowed to step in the way.
blocks.solvedMessage: Qe8# — the pinned rook could not interpose on f8. ✓
blocks.wrongMessage: Not that one — strike where the defender cannot interpose.

blocks.text: A **skewer** is a pin turned around: the more valuable piece stands **in front**, the lesser one behind it. In a pin the front piece may not step aside; in a skewer it must — and in stepping aside it exposes what was behind it. That is why a skewer is almost always played **with check**, because then the king has no choice. These two motifs are the ones most often confused, and the only difference is which of the two stands in front.

blocks.title: Rook skewer
blocks.hint: Check the king so that what stands behind it is left on its own.
blocks.solvedMessage: Rh8+ and Rxa8 — wherever the king goes. ✓
blocks.wrongMessage: Not that one — the king has to step off the line.
blocks.playingPrompt: Play the move that sets up the skewer.

blocks.text: In a **discovered attack** the piece that moves is not the piece that strikes. It merely takes itself off the line, and the threat arrives from the piece behind it. That is what makes it so dangerous: your opponent looks at the thing that moved and overlooks the thing that actually threatened. When what stands behind is the **king**, a discovered attack becomes a **discovered check** — the sharpest form, because your opponent must answer the check and has no time for anything else. And when the piece stepping aside attacks something of its own as well, one move puts two threats on the board.

blocks.title: Who is really giving mate?
blocks.hint: The piece that delivers mate should not move — it needs its path opened.
blocks.solvedMessage: e7# — mate is given by the bishop on d5. ✓
blocks.wrongMessage: Not that one — open the bishop's diagonal.
blocks.playingPrompt: Play the move that uncovers the attack.

blocks.title: Motifs are recognised, not memorised
blocks.text: An eye that has seen a fork a hundred times finds it before it can calculate it. So after this lesson move on to the **Puzzles** tab — a new position to solve is waiting there every day.
